'''Fay Ajzenberg-Selove''' (February 13, 1926{{spaced ndash}}August 8, 2012) was an American [[nuclear physicist]].  She was known for her experimental work in [[nuclear spectroscopy]] of light elements, and for her annual reviews of the energy levels of light atomic nuclei. She was a recipient of the 2007 [[National Medal of Science]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.upenn.edu/pennnews/news/penn-physicist-fay-ajzenberg-selove-among-eight-scientists-receive-2007-national-medal-science |title=Penn Physicist Fay Ajzenberg-Selove Among Eight Scientists to Receive the 2007 National Medal of Science &#124; Penn News |publisher=Upenn.edu |date=2008-08-26 |access-date=2012-09-08 |archive-date=2012-02-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120229235335/http://www.upenn.edu/pennnews/news/penn-physicist-fay-ajzenberg-selove-among-eight-scientists-receive-2007-national-medal-science |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.philly.com/2012-09-05/news/33583139_1_physics-bok-read-professor |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121114040248/http://articles.philly.com/2012-09-05/news/33583139_1_physics-bok-read-professor |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 14, 2012 |title=Physics professor Ajzenberg-Selove; honored by U.S. - Philly.com |publisher=Articles.philly.com |access-date=2012-09-08}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
She was born '''Fay Ajzenberg''' on 13 February 1926 in [[Berlin, Germany]] to a [[Polish Jews|Polish Jewish family]] from the [[Russian Empire]].  Her father, Moisei Abramovich Aisenberg (Polish: Mojzesz Ajzenberg), was a mining engineer who studied at the [[St. Petersburg School of Mines]] and her mother, Olga Ajzenberg ''[[née]]'' Naiditch, was a pianist and [[mezzo-soprano]] who studied at the St. Petersburg Academy of Music.<ref>[https://www.encyclopedia.com/women/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/ajzenberg-selove-fay-1926 "Ajzenberg-Selove, Fay (1926—)"], citing Ajzenberg-Selove, Fay. ''A Matter of Choices: Memoirs of a Female Physicist'', NJ: Rutgers University Press, 1994.</ref> In 1919, they fled the [[Russian Revolution (1917)|Russian Revolution]] and settled in Germany, where her father became a wealthy investment banker.<ref name="wcp">{{cite encyclopedia | title=Fay Ajzenberg-Selove | encyclopedia=Women in Chemistry and Physics: A Biobibliographic Sourcebook | publisher=Greenwood Press | author=McLane, Victoria | editor1=Grinstein, Louise S. | editor2=Rose, Rose K. | editor-link3=Miriam Rafailovich | editor3=Rafailovich, Miriam H. | year=1993 | isbn=978-0-313-27382-7 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/womeninchemistry00grin/page/1 1–8] | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/womeninchemistry00grin/page/1 }}</ref>

They were bankrupted by the [[Great Depression]], so the family moved to [[France]] in 1930.  Her father worked as a chemical engineer in a [[sugar beet]] factory owned by her uncle Isaac Naiditch in [[Lieusaint, Seine-et-Marne]], France.  Ajzenberg attended the [[Lycée Victor Duruy]] in [[Paris]] and Le [[Collège Sévigné]]. In 1940, the family fled Paris prior to the [[Battle of France|Nazi invasion of France]].  They took a tortuous route through [[Spain]], [[Portugal]], the [[Dominican Republic]], and [[Cuba]] before they settled in [[New York City]] in April 1941.<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa">Shalvi, Alice. [http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/ajzenberg-selove-fay "Fay Ajzenberg-Selove."] ''Jewish Women: A Comprehensive Historical Encyclopedia''. 1 March 2009. Jewish Women's Archive. Retrieved July 5, 2011</ref>

Ajzenberg graduated from [[Julia Richman High School]] in 1943. Her father had encouraged her interest in engineering.<ref name="Lubkin2013">{{cite journal|last=Lubkin|first=Gloria|title=Fay Ajzenberg-Selove|journal=Physics Today |year=2013 |volume=66|issue=6|page=62 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.2018|bibcode = 2013PhT....66f..62L |doi-access=free}}</ref> She attended the [[University of Michigan]], where she was friends with Haitian president [[François Duvalier|"Papa Doc" Duvalier]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Anleitner |first1=Joselyn |author2=Kaitlyn Beyer |author3=Candyce Boyd |work=A Series of Firsts: Women in Michigan Science and Engineering, 1940-1985 |publisher=University of Michigan Women in Science & Engineering |year=2011 |title=Fay Ajzenberg-Selove (Interview audio and transcript) |url=http://www.umich.edu/~whimse/selove.html |access-date=30 July 2013}}
</ref> She graduated in 1946 with a BS in engineering, the only woman in a class of 100.  After briefly doing graduate work in physics at [[Columbia University]] and teaching at the University of Illinois at Navy Pier, she began doctoral studies at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].

At Wisconsin she worked with nuclear physicist Hugh Richards who was studying nuclear reaction energies and classifying the energy levels of light atoms.<ref>{{cite web |title=On the Death of Professor Emeritus Hugh T. Richards |url=http://www.secfac.wisc.edu/senate/2007/0507/1986(mem_res).pdf |publisher=University of Wisconsin |date=7 May 2007 |access-date=9 August 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111209045633/https://www.secfac.wisc.edu/senate/2007/0507/1986(mem_res).pdf |archive-date=9 December 2011 }}</ref> She found a method of creating <sup>6</sup>[[Lithium|Li]] targets by converting the [[sulphate]] to a [[chloride]] and [[electroplating]] it to the target.  She also demonstrated that the [[excited state]]s of the <sup>10</sup>[[Boron|B]] [[Nucleus (atomic structure)|nucleus]] were not evenly spaced as previously thought.<ref name=wcp /> She received her MS in 1949 and her PhD in physics in 1952 with a dissertation titled "Energy levels of some light nuclei and their classification."<ref name="Lubkin2013" /> She was an atheist.<ref>Ajzenberg-Selove, Fay. A Matter of Choices: Memoirs of a Female Physicist. New Brunswick, NJ: Rutgers UP, 1994. Print. "I explained carefully to Louis that I was a Jew and an atheist..."</ref>

==Physics career==
She did [[postdoctoral]] work with [[Thomas Lauritsen]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]].  Together they would publish ''Energy Levels of Light Nuclei'', a compilation of the field's best yearly research regarding nuclear structure and decay of nuclei with an [[mass number|atomic mass number]] A from 5 to 20.  Since 1973 Ajzenberg published them herself.<ref name=wcp />  Eventually Ajzenberg would publish 26 of these papers, primarily in the journal ''[[Nuclear Physics (journal)|Nuclear Physics]]'', until 1990.  They have been called "the nuclear scientists' bible."<ref name="jwa"/>

Following graduation, Ajzenberg was a lecturer at [[Smith College]] and a visiting fellow at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. She was hired as an assistant professor of physics at [[Boston University]], but the dean lowered her salary 15 percent when he learned Ajzenberg was a woman. Ajzenberg refused the position until the initial salary was restored.<ref name=wcp />

While at Boston University, she met [[Harvard University]] physicist Walter Selove and they married in December 1955.<ref name=wcp /> One of her graduate students was [[Gloria Lubkin]], who graduated in 1957 with an MA in Nuclear Physics, and would later become the first female editor in chief of ''[[Physics Today]]''. In 2013, Lubkin wrote Ajzenberg's obituary as her final story for the magazine.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lubkin|first=Gloria B.|date=2013-05-31|title=Fay Ajzenberg-Selove|journal=Physics Today|volume=66|issue=6|pages=62|doi=10.1063/PT.3.2018|bibcode=2013PhT....66f..62L|issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1962, using the [[bubble chamber]] at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], Selove discovered a [[meson]] he named the [[List of mesons|fayon]] (f<sub>2</sub>) after her.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | title=Walter Selove | author1=Hagopian, Vasken | author2=Hagopian, Sharon | author3=Kononenko, Walter | journal=Physics Today | date=April 2011 | volume=64 | issue=4 | page=72 | doi=10.1063/1.3580502 | bibcode=2011PhT....64d..72H | doi-access=free }}</ref> Ajzenberg-Selove and her husband were honored with a symposium about their work at the University of Pennsylvania in 2005.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=gPGZJ_YuMwgC|title = American Women of Science Since 1900|last = Wayne|first = Tiffany K.|date = 2011-01-01|publisher = ABC-CLIO|isbn = 9781598841589|language = en}}</ref> Selove died in 2010.<ref name=":0"/>

In the 1960s, she worked at [[Haverford College]], where she was the first full-time female faculty member.<ref name="jwa"/> In 1970, Ajzenberg-Selove began teaching at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where Selove had taught since 1957.  In 1972, she applied for one of three [[tenure]]d positions there.<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa"/>  She was not hired; the reasons cited were age and "inadequate research publications".<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa"/>  Ajzenberg-Selove was only 46, had a [[Citation impact|citation count]] higher than everyone in the physics department except for [[Nobel Prize|Nobel]] laureate [[J. Robert Schrieffer]], and was Nuclear Physics Section chair of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa"/>  She filed complaints with the [[Equal Employment Opportunity Commission]] and the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission and in 1973 the University of Pennsylvania was ordered to give her a tenured professorship.<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa"/>  She became only the second female professor in the university's School of Arts and Sciences.<ref name=wcp /><ref name="jwa"/>

==Publications==
In 1994, she published a memoir, ''A Matter of Choices: Memoirs of a Female Physicist''.<ref name=":1"/>

== Honors and awards ==
* Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science
* Fellow, American Physical Society
* Chair,  American Physical Society Division of Nuclear Physics (1973–1974)
* Award for Distinguished Teaching, Christian and Mary Lindbeck Foundation (1991)
* Nicholson Medal for Humanitarian Service, American Physical Society (1999)
* Distinguished Alumni Fellow Award, University of Wisconsin Department of Physics (2001)
*[[National Medal of Science]] (2007)
